title: Good Leaders Presume Team Members Feel Undervalued and Underappreciated
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues busy leaders unintentionally leave team members, even top performers, feeling unseen because attention gets consumed by problems and results rather than people. The recommended discipline is presuming everyone -- especially the most talented -- feels less valued than they deserve, and deliberately building unstructured check-in time devoted purely to connection rather than project updates. The author closes by calling the simple act of making a team member feel important potentially the most consequential thing a leader does on any given day.
points: Busy leaders don't devalue team members on purpose, but their attention naturally drifts toward problems and results rather than people.
Counterintuitively, it's often the most talented and successful team members who need the most reassurance that they matter.
The recommended discipline is scheduling regular, unstructured check-in time that avoids discussing projects entirely.
The piece frames making each team member feel valued as potentially the single most consequential thing a leader does daily.
quotes: Given how busy leaders are and how focused they are on dealing with problems and delivering results, it is easy for team members to feel undervalued, unseen, and unimportant.
Surprisingly, it is often the most talented and successful team members who require the most reassurance that they matter.

The best leaders build a discipline of nurturing relationships and make people feel seen and important. They assume that others always feel less significant than they deserve, especially their top performers.
In these check-ins, they avoid discussing projects or team problems. Instead, they use the time simply to connect.
The simple act of making each team member feel important may be the most consequential thing a leader does on any given day.
